progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: a vector is a living carrier; dengue and malaria are vector-borne. From b09: immunity depends on memory cells specific to one antigen. From b10: herd immunity ("when enough people are immune, an infected person meets too few people who can catch it"). From b12: the Aedes aegypti container life cycle; eggs hatch after rain; adults in about a week; the virus multiplies in the mosquito for about 8 to 12 days; Wolbachia greatly reduces dengue transmission by Aedes, spreads by itself and keeps working after releases; Townsville's local cases in 2024 to 2025. From Year 11: reading a line graph and a percentage. Not assumed: incidence, prevalence, rate per 100,000, seroprevalence, serotypes, serotype-specific immunity, randomised trial design.
progression.startsWith: Read incidence and prevalence data for a named disease. The video opens: In 2021, a trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, reported seventy-seven per cent fewer dengue cases where Wolbachia mosquitoes had been released.
progression.stopsAfter: naming dengue (caused by a virus with four serotypes, spread mainly by *Aedes aegypti*, which breeds in containers) as the named disease, with malaria (caused by *Plasmodium*, a protozoan parasite, spread by *Anopheles*) as the alternative; defining incidence (new cases in a set time per number of people) and prevalence (the share of a population that has a disease at one time), and explaining why dengue's prevalence stays low while past infection, a separate measure from antibodies (seroprevalence), is high (about seven in ten urban Indonesian children in 2014); comparing places by rate per 100,000 (cases divided by population, times 100,000), not by counts; reading a seasonal incidence graph and explaining the lag after the rains (breeding, then the virus's time in the mosquito); explaining why serotype-specific immunity lets outbreaks happen in mostly immune cities and why second infections can be more severe and why a vaccine must cover all four serotypes; explaining how mobility carries serotypes between cities and starts north Queensland outbreaks; analysing transmission as four conditions that must all be met (virus, *Aedes*, warmth and water for breeding, non-immune people in contact; cut one far enough and spread stops) and the social causes that shape them (water storage, crowded growing cities, funding and community support); interpreting the Yogyakarta randomised trial (about 2 in 100 against about 9 in 100 febrile clinic patients with dengue; 77 per cent lower) and the Cairns comparison over time (about 96 per cent lower), and judging which is stronger evidence (Cairns had no untreated areas compared at the same time); combining biological and social causes to explain why dengue control is still limited.
progression.nextLesson: practise reading outbreak data and choosing controls (route entry bio-m7-g01).

teaching.task: A randomised trial in Yogyakarta found about 77 per cent fewer dengue cases where Wolbachia mosquitoes were released, yet 2024 set a record for dengue cases reported to WHO. What limits dengue control, and how do incidence and prevalence data show it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why prevalence of current dengue is low but past infection high (short illness, no drain for past infection; 3, 4); why rates beat counts (population size; 4); why the peak trails the rain (breeding time plus the virus's time in the mosquito; 5); why a mostly immune city still has outbreaks (serotype-specific immunity; 6); why second infections can be worse and vaccines hard (6); how outbreaks start in Australia (travellers; 7); why removing one condition stops spread, and how social causes feed each condition (8); why a randomised trial is stronger than before-and-after (9); why control is still limited (10). Visible case: the same four-conditions bar gains causes and breaks; the same map carries the trial, travel and Cairns. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 9 (two studies) and 10 (two columns) are the densest, so items dim as the next writes.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In 2021 a randomised trial in Yogyakarta reported about 77 per cent fewer dengue cases where Wolbachia mosquitoes had been released, yet 2024 set a record for dengue cases reported worldwide, so the question is what limits malaria or dengue control, using dengue in South East Asia as the named disease. Dengue is a virus spread mainly by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes breeding in water containers, with four serotypes. Incidence is new cases in a set time for a set number of people, and prevalence is the share of a population that has the disease at a time; because dengue illness lasts about a week, prevalence stays low even in a big outbreak, while past infection is measured separately by antibody surveys, and comparisons use rates per 100,000 people. One city's weekly incidence stays low in the dry months and climbs after the wet season starts. Immunity covers only the serotype that caused it, so herd immunity against one serotype does not stop a new one, and mobility carries the virus between cities within a day. Dengue spreads when the virus, Aedes mosquitoes, warmth and water, and non-immune people meet, and people shape each condition. The Yogyakarta cluster trial is strong evidence, but releases take years, money and residents' consent, so control stays limited. The memory aid is incidence is the tap, prevalence is the tank. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 2021, a trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, reported seventy-seven per cent fewer dengue cases where Wolbachia mosquitoes had been released. Yet in 2024, countries reported more dengue than ever recorded, over fourteen million cases. So if one method works that well, what limits dengue control?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a is an interpret item with counts and populations (incidence per 100,000; the route start). 12c is an explain item with serosurvey and mobility data (the portion immune and mobility, the syllabus's own example). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ4-01 (p 55): "investigate and analyse the wide range of interrelated factors involved in limiting local, regional and global spread of a named infectious disease" (named disease: dengue; local scale: breeding containers and household water storage, scene 8; regional: serotypes moving between South East Asian cities and into north Queensland, scenes 6 and 7; global: the 2024 record and climate, scenes 1 and 10; interrelated: the four conditions and the social causes shaping each, scene 8). B7-IQ4-05 (p 55): "interpret data relating to the incidence and prevalence of infectious disease in populations, for example:" with the listed examples "mobility of individuals and the portion that are immune or immunised (ACSBL124, ACSBL125)" (scenes 6 and 7, attempt 2) and "Malaria or Dengue Fever in South East Asia" (dengue in Indonesia carries the whole video). Verb "investigate and analyse": scene 8 relates factors to each other, scene 10 combines them. Verb "interpret": scenes 4, 5 and 9 read real and teaching data; both attempts are data items.

design.visualSystem: One four-conditions bar across the top from scene 2: four linked slots, "virus", "Aedes", "warmth and water", "people not immune", each with a small plate or coded glyph; slots light or break as scenes refer to them, and scene 8 adds a social cause under each. Below it, the data panel at the right half shows one dataset at a time (the tank, the rate bars, the weekly graph, the serotype grid, the trial grid). A coded map of South East Asia and northern Australia (outline only, no labels except the named places) sits at the left in scenes 1, 2, 7 and 9, with dots for Yogyakarta, Cairns and Townsville. People are never drawn: populations are coded dot grids (plain circles), coloured by serotype immunity in scene 6. The dengue virus is the new painted `m7-dengue-virus-v1.png`, its four serotypes shown as four colour rings on the same plate (one plate, four tints applied in code as outline rings, never recolouring the painting). No people, hands or faces: no patients, clinicians, families, travellers or crowds; travel is a coded arc between map dots; the clinic is a coded building outline. Scale: the virus, the mosquito, the jar and the Wolbachia cell are never shown at one scale; each has a grey label, and the virus carries "drawn far larger than real (about 50 nanometres)". Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.

scenes.onScreenChange: the card writes on as an exam question, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "In 2022, a survey in City R, where *Aedes aegypti* is common, found that 80% of adults had antibodies from a past dengue infection. Almost all of these infections had been caused by dengue serotype 1 (DENV-1). Piped water in City R is often cut off, so most households store water in open jars. In 2025, dengue serotype 3 (DENV-3) was detected in travellers arriving in City R, and the city then had its largest dengue outbreak in ten years, with a higher proportion of severe cases than in earlier outbreaks." Demand: "Explain the 2025 outbreak, with reference to biological and social factors in the data. (4 marks)". One lined answer box. No plates. **The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds.** The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.
